passage:
January, a quiet Sunday. Ira wrote a rule on an index card: "If shares fall so that they are much less of my mix, move a small slice from the steady holdings into shares." She stuck it inside the notebook.
March, the week of the crash. Ira's shares had dropped and the mix had drifted. Lokesh, her friend, texted, "You're not actually buying more now, are you?" Ira read the card twice. "I wrote this when I was calm," she replied. Her hands were cold as she moved the slice.
April. Prices were still unsteady, but the mix was back near the plan. Ira added a line to the card: "Review once a year." Lokesh sent a thumbs-up.

qa.q: Where did Ira keep the rule?
qa.a: Ira kept the rule inside the notebook.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when moving the slice in March?
qa.a: Ira was nervous, shown by the cold hands, but held to the card because she wrote it while calm.

qa.q: What could Ira do if she started to doubt the rule during a fall?
qa.a: Ira could talk it over with a registered adviser before changing the card, rather than changing it in the heat of the moment.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt seeing Ira follow the card?
qa.a: Lokesh was worried at first, given the sharp text, and later relieved enough to send a thumbs-up.

grounding: The passage shows an investor following a rule written in a calm period by moving a small share into equity when the mix drifts.

passage:
Siddharth Mama took a folded paper from his old wallet when Ira asked how he had stayed calm in crashes. "I wrote this at twenty-five, after my first job. 'Seventy percent in shares, thirty in safe deposits. If either side drifts more than five points, move it back. Check once a year, in March.' That's all.
The first test came two years later. The market crashed. My share part had dropped to sixty percent. Every newspaper said sell. My heart said sell. But the paper said: move money from the safe side into shares, back to seventy. So I did, in small steps, over two months. It felt terrible, like throwing money into a fire.
Three years later, that was the best money I ever put in. Not because I was clever. Because I decided when I was calm, and obeyed the paper when I was scared."

qa.q: When did Siddharth check his mix each year?
How did young Siddharth feel moving money into shares during the crash?
qa.a: It felt terrible, like throwing money into a fire; he was frightened but followed his written rule.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Writing the rule when calm and following it when scared, because it stopped fear from making the decision.

qa.q: What would have changed if he had followed the newspapers?
qa.a: He would likely have sold near the bottom and missed what became his best investment.

grounding: It shows a young investor following a rule written in calm times, moving a small share from safe deposits back into shares when the mix drifts during a crash.

passage:
Farida's rule sat in a note on her phone, written two years earlier with help from Amandeep, a friend who was a registered adviser: "Target 60% shares, 40% debt funds. If shares drift below 55% or above 65%, move back to 60. Only on the first working day of a quarter."
On 1 April the market had fallen hard, and her share portion had slipped to 52 percent. The complication: Farida was at a client site in rural Odisha for two weeks, with one bar of signal and a laptop that kept dying.
She could have waited until she got back, when things looked calmer. Instead, at 6 am, standing on the guest-house roof where the signal was best, she moved enough from her debt fund into shares to bring it back to 60. It took twenty minutes and three dropped connections.
She didn't look at the market again until July.

qa.q: What share of her money did Farida's rule target for shares?
What might Farida have felt on the guest-house roof at 6 am?
qa.a: She may have felt uneasy moving money into a falling market, but determined to follow the rule set when she was calm.

qa.q: What made Farida's rule easy to follow even in a crisis?
qa.a: It was written in advance with clear numbers and a fixed date, so she didn't have to make an emotional judgement.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Farida's choice?
qa.a: Amandeep, who helped write the rule, would likely be glad she followed it despite the crash and the poor signal.

grounding: It shows an investor rebalancing from debt funds into shares when the mix drifts in a crash, following a rule written earlier despite poor signal on a work trip.
